meaning: to start planning again from the beginning after a plan has failed
example: The first prototype failed every test, so the team went back to the drawing board.
origin: From architecture and engineering, where designs are drawn on a drawing board; the figurative use became common in the 20th century

wrong_meanings.meaning: to draw a picture of a board game
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: The idiom is figurative and does not refer to games or drawings. It describes restarting a plan after a failure.

wrong_meanings.meaning: to hang a finished painting on a wall
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: This is the opposite of the idiom. It refers to presenting a completed work, while the idiom describes returning to the start after failing.

wrong_meanings.meaning: to return a lost object to its owner
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: The idiom has nothing to do with returning objects. It describes beginning a planning process again.

explanation: 'Back to the drawing board' means that an approach has failed and the work must be planned again from the start.
